# Lance fixtures

Datasets that the `lance_fdw` regression suites read, plus the reference output
they are checked against. Everything here is produced by pylance —
nothing is hand-written.

```
gen_fixtures.py     generator: writes data/, expected/*.jsonl and manifest.json
upload_minio.py     syncs data/ into the S3 bucket used by the s3:// cases
manifest.json       what each dataset contains (committed, reviewable)
expected/<name>.jsonl   one JSON object per row, read back with pylance (committed)
data/<name>.lance/  the datasets themselves (gitignored, regenerated)
```

```sh
make gen                      # regenerate everything except 'big'
make gen GEN_FLAGS=--with-big # ... including the timing dataset
make upload                   # push data/ to s3://$LANCE_S3_BUCKET/fixtures/
make test                     # pytest; generates data/ first if it is missing
```

`make test` and `python3 -m pytest test/fixtures -q` are the same
thing. The tests regenerate the fixtures into a temporary directory and compare
byte for byte, so a generator change that would invalidate the committed
reference fails there.

## Datasets

| name | rows | fragments | what it is for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `types_all` | 24 | 3 | Every A-tier Arrow type, NULLs in every column. The per-column NULL pattern has period 7, so with 8 rows per fragment and `batch_size=3` the NULLs land at different in-batch offsets in every batch. The main fixture of the type suites. |
| `types_b` | 12 | 2 | B-tier columns (struct, dictionary, uint64, `list<list<int64>>`, `list<struct>`, duration) beside two A-tier ones, so `IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA` has something left after skipping them, and a hand-written foreign table can reference a B-tier column to get the type error. |
| `deleted` | 16 | 4 | Rows 0, 3, 11 and 19 deleted, leaving deletion files on fragments 0, 2 and 3 and none on fragment 1. Deleted rows must not appear, and the resulting sliced batches have non-zero `array->offset`. |
| `empty` | 0 | 0 | Schema, no data. pylance writes no fragment at all, so every QE gets an empty share. |
| `frag_1` … `frag_100` | 5 … 100 | 1, 2, 3, 7, 100 | Fragment-count coverage for the 3-segment modulo split: fewer fragments than segments, exactly as many, and far more. All fragments are the same size, so per-segment row counts are predictable. `frag_100` holds one row per fragment to keep the reference file small. |
| `frag_gap` | 15 | 3 | Fragment 1 deleted whole. Surviving fragment ids are 0, 2, 3 — nothing may assume ids are dense or start at 0. |
| `evolved` | 20 | 4 | Two `add_columns` calls (`v10 = id * 10`, `vup = upper(v)`), so each fragment's columns live in three data files. |
| `blob` | 4 | 2 | MiB-sized payloads twice: a plain `large_binary` column and one carrying Lance's `lance-encoding: blob` field metadata. Values are 1 MiB, empty, NULL and 2 MiB. |
| `large_text` | 8 | 2 | `large_utf8` from empty to 1 MiB, including `漢字`-repeats where byte length and character length differ, next to a short `utf8` column. |
| `versions` | 35 | 3 | Three versions of 10, 20 and 35 rows, append-only, for version pinning. |
| `nested` | 6 | 2 | A-tier `struct` in four shapes: flat `struct<a int32, b utf8>`, nested two deep, `list<struct>`, and a struct holding a `list<int32>`. NULLs at every level — whole value, subfield, list element and a NULL list inside a live struct. A2's main fixture. |
| `nested_btier` | 4 | 1 | `struct<ok int32, bad uint64>`: one B-tier subfield, so the whole column is B tier. `ok` on its own is A tier, which is what makes the refusal a decision rather than an accident — there is no partial projection of a struct. |
| `maps` | 5 | 2 | `map<utf8,int32>` (A tier → `jsonb`) beside `map<int32,utf8>` (B tier). Same Arrow shape, opposite verdicts. Written at Lance 2.2, the only format pylance 11 writes a map into. |
| `blobv2` | 4 | 2 | A Blob v2 column — `struct<data large_binary, uri utf8>` tagged `ARROW:extension:name = lance.blob.v2` — beside two A-tier columns. B tier by an explicit rule. Written at Lance 2.2, which Blob v2 requires. |
| `big` | opt-in | 3 | Wall-time comparison only: `--with-big` writes 3 fragments of 512 rows × 1 MiB. Random payloads, no expected output, not regenerated byte for byte. |

Every dataset's first column is a non-null `id` that ascends across fragments,
and `expected/<name>.jsonl` is in that order, so SQL cases compare against it
with `ORDER BY id`.

`manifest.json` records, per dataset: row count, fragment ids and their row
counts (before and after deletions), which fragments carry a deletion file, how
many data files each fragment has, the version history with row counts, and the
Lance file format version — plus, per column, the Arrow type, the Arrow C data
interface format string that lance-c and nanoarrow will see, the tier
and the PG type an A-tier column should import as.

## Tiers for the nested types

`classify()` in the generator is where the fixtures and the FDW agree on which
columns are readable. Three rules cover the nested types, and none of them has a
fallback — anything unnamed is B tier, never "probably A" and never "jsonb
because we don't know":

- **struct** is A tier only if *every* subfield is, recursively. One B-tier
  subfield makes the whole column B tier; a struct is read whole or not at all.
- **`map<K,V>`** is A tier only if `K` is `utf8`/`large_utf8` and `V` is an
  A-tier *scalar*. Anything else would have to be stringified or flattened to
  become a `jsonb` object, which is silent distortion.
- **Blob v2** — a field tagged `ARROW:extension:name = lance.blob.v2` — is
  always B tier. This one is spelled out rather than left to fall through: a v2
  descriptor is a struct of five A-tier scalars, so the struct rule alone would
  make it A tier and the FDW would hand out file offsets as if they were the
  payload.

A PostgreSQL composite type is named after the foreign table `IMPORT` creates,
so that name does not exist when the fixtures are generated. An A-tier struct
therefore records `"pg_type": "composite"` plus an ordered `composite_fields`,
`[[subfield name, pg_type], …]`; a subfield that is itself a struct keeps its own
`pg_type` and carries its own pairs in a third slot, so the shape is recoverable
without parsing `arrow_type`. `list<struct>` is `"composite[]"` and describes its
element. A-tier maps record `"pg_type": "jsonb"` and no `composite_fields`.
Only A-tier structs carry the key at all.

Two columns of `types_b` — `c_struct` and `c_list_struct` — became A tier when
`classify()` learned the struct rule. Their `purpose` and `notes` text in
`manifest.json` still calls them B-tier, and still says a map column is
impossible; both strings are frozen by the A1 contract and are stale. The
`schema` block below them is the authority.

## Expected output format

One JSON object per line, keys in schema order, ASCII-escaped:

| Arrow type | spelling |
|---|---|
| NULL (any type) | `null` |
| bool | `true` / `false` |
| all integers | JSON number |
| float16/32/64 | JSON number with Python's shortest round-trip repr; `"NaN"`, `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"` as strings, because JSON has no literals for them |
| decimal128(p,s) | string, never scientific notation, scale preserved (`"0.0000000000"`) |
| date32 | `"YYYY-MM-DD"` |
| timestamp | ISO-8601 with exactly as many fractional digits as the Arrow unit; tz-aware values are converted to UTC and suffixed `Z`, naive values carry no suffix |
| utf8 / large_utf8 | JSON string |
| binary / large_binary | lowercase hex string |
| fixed_size_list / list | JSON array of encoded elements |
| struct | JSON object, keys in subfield order; a NULL struct is `null`, a struct of NULLs is an object of `null`s |
| map | JSON array of `[key, value]` pairs — not an object, which is the only form that survives a non-string or repeated key |
| Blob v2 | the descriptor pylance returns (`{kind, position, size, blob_id, blob_uri}`), not the payload |
| B-tier columns | best-effort JSON; the FDW never reads these |

`manifest.json`'s `expected_format` legend still describes the `json` encoding as
"B-tier column"; A-tier structs and maps share it, because their values encode
identically either way and the legend is frozen.

A string or binary column whose longest value exceeds
`digest_threshold_bytes` (4096) is written as `{"chars", "bytes", "md5"}` /
`{"bytes", "md5"}` instead of the literal value — that is `blob.plain_lb`,
`blob.blob` and `large_text.txt`. SQL compares those with `octet_length()`,
`length()` and `md5()`; every other column is compared literally. Which
encoding a column got is recorded in `manifest.json` as `expected_encoding`.

## Things pylance 11.0.0 decided for us

Recorded here because they shape what the later packages can test. The file
format each dataset was written in is in `manifest.json`
(`data_storage_version`, `file_format_versions`); pass
`--data-storage-version 2.0` to the generator if lance-c turns out not to read
2.1.

- **A `map` column needs Lance 2.2.** One was wanted in `types_b`
  and did not get it: pylance 11 refuses Arrow `map` at 2.0 (*"Lance v2.0 has no
  field encoding for 'c' with data type Map"*), at 2.1 and at its own default
  (*"Map data type is not enabled by the selected file format"*). It writes one
  at **2.2**, which is why `maps` is a separate dataset pinned to that format
  rather than another column of `types_b`. Arrow `month_day_nano_interval` is
  rejected in every format (*"Unsupported data type: Interval(MonthDayNano)"*),
  so duration stands in for the interval/duration row of the B-tier list.
- **A dataset may pin its own file format.** `Built.storage_version` overrides
  both pylance's default and `--data-storage-version`, because some shapes exist
  in exactly one format and pinning 2.0 across the board must not silently
  produce a dataset pylance cannot write. Only `maps` and `blobv2` use it.
- **Blob v1 and Blob v2 cannot share a storage version.** The v1 spelling
  (`lance-encoding: blob` on a `large_binary`) is refused from 2.2 on — *"Legacy
  blob columns … are not supported for file version >= 2.2"* — and the v2
  extension type is refused below it — *"Blob v2 requires file version >= 2.2"*.
  Hence `blob` at 2.1 and `blobv2` at 2.2.
- **Blob v2 is an extension type, not a threshold.** The
  `lance-encoding:blob-*-size-threshold` keys only choose inline / packed /
  dedicated storage; on their own they leave an ordinary `large_binary` column.
  What makes a column v2 is the field type `struct<data: large_binary, uri:
  utf8>` plus `ARROW:extension:name = lance.blob.v2`. Importing `lance`
  registers that extension, so pyarrow folds the tag into an `ExtensionType` on
  read-back and the metadata key disappears; `classify()` accepts either
  spelling. `to_table()` then returns a five-child descriptor rather than the
  bytes, which is the opposite of what v1 does (below).
- **No zero-row fragment.** Deleting every row of a fragment makes Lance drop
  the fragment, and `LanceFragment.create()` rejects empty input, so `frag_gap`
  can only offer a hole in the fragment id sequence. The "a QE gets no rows"
  case is covered by `empty` and by `frag_1`/`frag_2` on three segments.
- **Blobs come back inlined.** Reading the `lance-encoding: blob` column with
  `to_table()` returns the bytes, not a position/size descriptor — that is
  the answer from the Python side only; what lance-c's scanner returns is
  checked by the type suites.
- **`pa.string()` stays `utf8` and `pa.large_string()` stays `large_utf8`**
  through a write/read round trip, as do `binary`/`large_binary`,
  `float16`, `decimal128`, `fixed_size_list` and timestamp zone names.
- **Timestamps in `types_all` are microsecond-aligned on purpose.** PG stores
  microseconds, so an A-tier read of a nanosecond column must be exact; a value
  with sub-microsecond digits would have to be an error instead, which is a
  different test than "equals pylance".
